newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries close higher, Fed anxiety fades.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries close higher, Fed anxiety fades.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries closed higher for the first time in four sessions on Monday as investors bought on a renewed view that monetary policy is likely to remain unchanged in the near term, analysts said.
The 6-1/2-percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended up 20/32 at 100-15/32. Its yield slipped to 6.46 percent against the 6.51 percent registered at the close on Friday.
"There's a renewed sentiment the Fed will remain on hold, absolutely," said Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.
The market was rattled late last week after the chairman of the Federal Reserve Alan Greenspan said the Fed must be wary when irrational exuberance affects stocks and assets.
Prices dropped on fears the Fed could raise interest rates in a bid to curb a speculative bubble in the stock market.
Those fears, however, had mostly faded by the opening of the market on Monday. "I don't think Greenspan would consider hiking rates to curb a rise in stocks," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.

The consensus among players by the close of business on Monday indicated that what Greenspan attempted to do with his comments last Thursday was to bring the markets down with words rather than actions.
"I think we might expect further comments from him going forward because there's a feeling Greenspan truly believes the stock market has become too frothy," the trader added.
The Fed last changed interest rates in January, when it cut its target for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to the current 5.25 percent level.
Analysts also said economic fundamentals have not been playing a major role in the U.S. debt market lately.
They said trading has become more technical, adding that money flows, mainly from foreign accounts, have been responsible for most of the recent price action.
"Recent economic data have not been strong enough to change people's minds about the economy," said the head of money market desk at a U.S. investment bank.
"So the market has become more technical ... and volatile. People have been trading on flows and, more recently, on Greenspan's comments," he added.
Pundits said most of the gains Monday were triggered by strong corporate buying, mainly from trust funds in Japan.
"There was some overseas buying ... but domestic accounts were pretty much dead in the water," said Jerry Zukowski, money market economist at PaineWebber.
Analysts noted some very scattered activity by hedge and mutual funds on Monday, while retailers were said to be mostly out of the market.
Interest rate swaps and some activity in the Eurodollar market also helped prices. A better performance of the greenback against other currencies also provided support.
On Monday, the market also took in $26.0 billion in three- and six-month Treasury bills. The securities were placed at 4.83 percent and 4.97 percent, respectively.
Analysts said the market is likely to remain rangebound over the next few days as players await the November wholesale and retail inflation data, due out on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.
Experts see yields on the bellwether 30-year bond trading within a range between 6.40 and 6.60 percent.
The three-month Treasury bill rate closed down five basis points to 4.85 percent.
The six-month bill rate fell three points to 4.99 percent. The year bill rate was off three points at 5.13 percent.

The two-year note closed up 2/32 at 99-28/32, yielding 5.69 percent. The five-year note traded up 6/32 at 99-21/32 to yield 5.96 percent. The ten-year note closed up 14/32 at 102-9/32, yielding 6.19 percent.
